items.title: Vince Giordano interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2007
items.q: Mr. Morton, Jelly Roll Morton said if you’ve got a half a glass of water you can go up.

ctx.x: But the music of, you know Goldkette —

Yeah, or Jelly Roll Morton. Because I think it’s the hip thing to do. You know there’s not too many hip folks that are probably going to want to listen to some ancient acoustic recording or a recording that’s three minutes long or a recording that musicians had to work in a certain framework. You know there wasn’t much freedom on a jazz recording in 1927 than there was in 1957. And it is what it is. You know there’s no great dissonances in Mozart and it’s beautiful the way it is. And your early automobiles…

early jazz masters were the pioneers. Before them, for the most part, there was no jazz. You know there were people doing classical music and folk music and pop music and here was these fellows and gals saying I’m creating a new language and this is great. Of course not everything that came from those times or those musicians is golden, I understand that. But there’s a lot of great stuff there.
